evidence: Sen. Ep. 124.16: cum ad initium ejus admōtus est
terms.comment: As for “his” and “her”: when the owner is not the subject. tamquam equus reminīscitur viae cum ad initium ejus admōtus est, the start of it, of the road.

evidence: Cic. Sen. 52: claviculīs suīs quasi manibus
terms.comment: When the owner is the subject: the vine claviculīs suīs … complectitur, holds on with its tendrils. Gellius shows both in one sentence: the Gauls call the wind that blows ex suā terrā (their own land) after turbine ejus (its whirling).

phrases.latin: tamquam equus reminīscitur viae cum ad initium ejus admōtus est
phrases.english: as a horse remembers a road when it is brought to the start of it

phrases.latin: nostrī namque Gallī ventum ex suā terrā flantem, quem saevissimum patiuntur, circium appellant ā turbine, opīnor, ejus ac vertīgine
phrases.english: For our Gauls call the wind that blows from their own land, which they find the fiercest, circius, from its whirling and turning, I think.

phrases.latin: vītis quidem, quae nātūrā cadūca est et, nisi fulta est, fertur ad terram, eadem, ut sē ērigat, claviculīs suīs quasi manibus quicquid est nacta complectitur
phrases.english: The vine, which by nature droops and falls to the ground unless it is propped, raises itself by clasping with its tendrils, as with hands, whatever it finds.

phrases.latin: et latet et lūcet Phaethontide condita guttā, ut videātur apis nectare clūsa suō
phrases.english: The bee lies hidden and shines, shut in a drop of amber, so that it seems enclosed in its own nectar.

sources: Lewis & Short: is · Lewis & Short: suus
